schools_affected: All LAUSD schools (district-wide, 750+ sites)
description: Voters overwhelmingly approved Measure RR, a $7 billion general obligation bond for school facility improvements, with nearly 71% support (55% threshold required). Funds designated for upgrading 70% of district facilities in need of repairs, replacing aging HVAC and plumbing systems, retrofitting buildings, installing security and communication systems, and accessibility upgrades. More than 77% of LAUSD's 750 school sites are at least 50 years old and 13% are 100+ years old. Bond extends existing tax rate of $21.74 per $100,000 assessed value through 2055, raising ~$329 million annually.

schools_affected: All LAUSD schools (district-wide)
description: LA voters overwhelmingly approved Measure US, LAUSD's largest-ever school facilities bond at $9 billion, with 68% of the vote. The bond will fund repair and upgrade of aging school buildings, addressing more than $80 billion in unfunded school facility and technology needs. More than 60% of LAUSD campuses are at least a half-century old. Cost to property owners estimated at $25.04 per $100,000 of assessed value per year. Supported by the school board, Superintendent Carvalho, UTLA, and local construction groups.

schools_affected: N/A - measure failed
description: LAUSD Measure EE, a parcel tax of 16 cents per square foot that would have raised approximately $500 million annually for 12 years, was decisively defeated by voters in a June 2019 special election. The measure received only 45.68% support, falling far short of the required two-thirds supermajority. The tax was considered vital to cover costs of salary agreements made with UTLA to resolve the January 2019 teachers' strike. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association had filed a lawsuit to block the election, but it became moot after voter rejection.

schools_affected: 32nd Street USC Magnets; Los Angeles High School; Wilmington Middle School STEAM Magnet
description: The LAUSD Board of Education approved more than $195.7 million in bond-funded projects for facility upgrades. The 32nd Street USC Magnets received approval for a $108 million multi-phase modernization project to construct 23 new general and specialty classrooms (media, filmmaking, engineering, graphic design, chemistry lab), plus exterior improvements, greening, landscaping, infrastructure, and ADA upgrades. The Board also approved $45 million for wellness center facilities at Los Angeles High School and Wilmington Middle School STEAM Magnet.

schools_affected: Ulysses S. Grant High School; Shenandoah Elementary School; North Hollywood High School; Multiple campuses (650+ projects in pre-construction)
description: LAUSD's Facilities Services Division was managing 650+ projects in pre-construction valued at $3.7 billion and 220 projects under construction valued at $1.6 billion. Notable projects included the nearly $150 million comprehensive modernization of Grant High School (completion targeted 2024) and the $54 million upgrade of Shenandoah Elementary (targeted completion end of 2023). North Hollywood High School underwent comprehensive modernization including seismic upgrade of ~100,000 SF and construction of a new classroom building, auditorium, and gymnasium. Over 120 new bond program projects were planned for bid between June 2020 and June 2021.

schools_affected: All LAUSD schools (district-wide, temporary)
description: LAUSD closed all schools in March 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, affecting approximately 600,000+ students at the time. The district extended closures through the remainder of the 2019-20 school year and continued remote learning into the 2020-21 school year. LAUSD was one of the last major urban districts to reopen for in-person instruction, not fully returning until spring 2021. The district invested in ventilation upgrades, though a June 2020 GAO study found 40% of schools nationwide needed HVAC updates or replacements.

schools_affected: Palisades Charter Elementary School; Marquez Charter Elementary School; Palisades Charter High School; Canyon Charter Elementary (adjacent to burn scar); Paul Revere Charter Middle School (adjacent to burn scar)
description: The January 2025 Palisades Fire destroyed or severely damaged three LAUSD schools. Marquez Elementary was burned to the ground. Palisades Elementary lost ~70% of its campus (17 classrooms, multipurpose room, play equipment). Palisades High lost ~30% (21 classrooms, storage, track and field). Students were relocated: 410 Palisades Elementary students to Brentwood Science Magnet, 312 Marquez students to Nora Sterry Elementary, and Palisades High students to a renovated Sears building in Santa Monica. Palisades Elementary enrollment dropped 25% post-fire.

schools_affected: Palisades Charter Elementary School (rebuild); Marquez Charter Elementary School (rebuild); Palisades Charter High School (rebuild)
description: The LAUSD Board of Education approved a $604 million plan to rebuild the three schools destroyed in the Palisades Fire. Reconstruction is set to conclude by end of 2028, restoring facilities for approximately 3,620 students. Funding comes primarily from the $9 billion Measure US bond approved by voters in November 2024, with $337.6 million earmarked for elementary school modernization and $266.6 million for high school upgrades. Designs incorporate wildfire resiliency as a core requirement, including fire-resistant concrete blocks, enhanced air filtration, and strategic landscaping.

schools_affected: Consolidations planned for 2027-28 (specific schools TBD)
description: LAUSD announced that budget cuts to school budgets will begin in the 2026-27 school year, with school consolidations and staffing reductions planned for the 2027-28 school year. The district contracted with consulting firm Ernst and Young to create models for closing and consolidating schools. LAUSD faces an estimated $1.6 billion deficit for 2027-28. In 2024-25, the district spent ~$2 billion more than revenue. Thirty-four schools have fewer than 200 students; nearly half of 456 zoned elementary schools are half-full or less; 56 have seen enrollment fall 70%+. Board member Tanya Ortiz Franklin called for a plan, while Board President Schmerelson acknowledged fear of community backlash.

schools_affected: All LAUSD Board of Education districts (political boundaries)
description: The LA City Council approved new LAUSD Board of Education district boundaries 14-0, following recommendations from the LAUSD Redistricting Commission. The map was nearly identical to the commission's recommendation, with one adjustment to keep Carver Middle School and Sally Ride Elementary School in District 5. The redistricting was required by the LA City Charter every 10 years based on updated census data.

schools_affected: ~200 school buildings placed off-limits to charter co-location
description: The LAUSD Board voted 4-3 to approve a new policy limiting charter school co-location under Proposition 39. The policy barred charter schools from sharing campuses with community schools, Black Student Achievement Plan (BSAP) schools, and the district's 100 schools targeted for academic improvement. Roughly 200 of the district's 770 school buildings were placed off-limits. UTLA supported the policy; the California Charter Schools Association opposed it and filed suit. In 2025, a judge ruled the policy violated Proposition 39 and reopened up to 346 school sites for potential charter co-locations.

schools_affected: All SDUSD schools (district-wide)
description: San Diego voters approved Measure U, a $3.2 billion general obligation bond measure, with 65.28% support. This was the district's fourth bond measure since 2008, bringing the total facilities bond program to $11.5 billion across Proposition S ($2.1B, 2008), Proposition Z ($2.8B, 2012), Measure YY ($3.4B, 2018), and Measure U. Funds support renovation, repair, and revitalization of school facilities including HVAC systems, new classroom buildings, roofs, parking lots, solar power systems, and athletic facilities. San Diego Unified pays the lowest interest rate of all districts in the state based on its most recent bond issuance.

schools_affected: Logan Memorial Educational Campus
description: San Diego Unified completed the Logan Memorial Educational Campus, a $100+ million TK-12 education complex in Logan Heights -- the first high school the neighborhood had ever had. The existing Logan K-8 and Memorial Prep campuses were rebuilt into a 241,000 sq ft campus on 19.8 acres with capacity for 2,060 students. The project won a 2023 CMAA Project Achievement Award. In December 2024, the district unveiled El Nido, a "cradle-to-college and career" infant/toddler Montessori Center at the campus, developed in partnership with Harvard University.

schools_affected: Civita Elementary School (planned new construction)
description: San Diego Unified approved plans to build a brand new elementary school in the Civita neighborhood of Mission Valley, where a population boom made a new school necessary. The district approved purchasing land from Civita developer Sudberry Properties for a 2-story, 24-classroom campus that will hold 500-600 students, located at Civita Boulevard and Via Alta. The district moved to secure the property after charter schools expressed interest in the site. Funding comes from voter-approved bond programs.

schools_affected: Hudson Elementary School (middle school grades eliminated)
description: The LBUSD Board of Education voted to eliminate middle school-grade offerings at Hudson Elementary in West Long Beach, citing dangerously low enrollment. The school's utilization rate had fallen below 20%. Hudson was originally built to host over 1,300 students. District-wide enrollment had fallen from ~75,000 in 2017-18 to below 64,000.

schools_affected: Hudson Elementary School (full closure)
description: The LBUSD Board of Education approved a plan to fully close Hudson Elementary at the end of the academic year. The West Long Beach campus enrolled only 231 students with just one teacher per grade level (K-5). Hudson was originally built for over 1,300 students. Starting in fall, the majority of Hudson students will attend Garfield Elementary School, about a half mile away. The closure is the latest symptom of declining enrollment district-wide.

schools_affected: All LBUSD schools (district-wide)
description: Long Beach voters passed a $1.7 billion bond measure allowing the district to upgrade schools by improving plumbing systems, maintaining safe drinking water, renovating facilities, and adding air conditioning systems. The bond is managed alongside existing Measure E, Measure K, and Measure Q programs with oversight from the Citizens' Bonds Oversight Committee. The district also adopted a sustainability plan in July 2022 to meet clean energy goals by 2045.

schools_affected: Long Beach Polytechnic High School
description: LBUSD kicked off the $450 million transformation of Long Beach Polytechnic High School (Poly), one of the district's most iconic campuses. The historic, multi-phase project is designed to reimagine the campus with new learning spaces and cutting-edge academic facilities. The project is made possible by voter-approved Measure Q and Measure E bond funds.

schools_affected: 17+ charter schools closed since 2019-20; Multiple Alliance for College-Ready Public Schools campuses; Multiple Green Dot Public Schools campuses
description: Across LA Unified's footprint, at least 17 charter schools have closed since the 2019-20 school year, with low enrollment as the typical common denominator. Some of the most prominent charter operators in LA -- including Alliance for College-Ready Public Schools and Green Dot Public Schools -- closed one or more campuses. Statewide in California, from 2021 to 2023, 31 new charter schools opened but 63 closed. National charter enrollment grew by 370,000 students between 2018-19 and 2020-21 even as traditional public school enrollment declined.

schools_affected: KIPP Pueblo Unido (Maywood, LAUSD-authorized); KIPP Generations Academy (Gardena, LAUSD-authorized); KIPP Poder Public School (Montebello, County-authorized)
description: On February 1, 2024, KIPP SoCal Public Schools board voted to close three of its schools due to low enrollment. KIPP Pueblo Unido and KIPP Generations were LAUSD-authorized; KIPP Poder was authorized by the LA County Board of Education. The closures reflect broader enrollment challenges facing both traditional public schools and charter networks in the region.

schools_affected: SEED LA Charter School (South Los Angeles)
description: The SEED LA Charter School project, a $97.4 million construction effort (including $70+ million in New Markets Tax Credit funding), closed financing in April 2021 with expected completion in January 2023. The project created a 147,479 sq ft educational facility comprising classrooms, offices, common areas, 20 staff apartments, and 170 dormitory units housing 400 students -- a public college-prep boarding high school in South LA providing STEM and humanities curriculum. Created 92 permanent jobs and 150 construction jobs.

schools_affected: Robeson High School (closed June 2018); Harper High School (phased out by 2021); Hope High School (phased out by 2021); TEAM Englewood High School (phased out by 2021)
description: The CPS Board voted unanimously to close four Englewood high schools over three years to make way for a new STEM school. Robeson closed immediately (June 2018) for construction of the replacement campus. Harper, Hope, and TEAM Englewood were phased out over three years so existing students could finish at their current schools. The closures came just after the expiration of a five-year moratorium on school closures imposed after the 2013 mass closures. More than 16 public schools have closed in Englewood since 2001.

schools_affected: Englewood STEM High School
description: Englewood STEM High School opened on September 3, 2019, as the first new school in the Englewood neighborhood since the 1970s. The $85 million state-of-the-art facility was built on the former Robeson campus and includes gleaming science labs, an 800-person gymnasium, sports fields, and specialized after-school programs. Upperclassmen can earn college credits through a partnership with Kennedy-King College. The school took in more than 400 freshmen its first year. It replaced four closed Englewood high schools that had suffered from declining enrollment, with ~90% of neighborhood students previously attending high schools outside of Englewood.

schools_affected: All CPS schools (district-wide, temporary)
description: Following Governor Pritzker's mandate, all CPS schools were closed from March 17, 2020, with the closure extended through the remainder of the 2019-20 school year (June 18, 2020). Students transitioned to remote learning. For the 2020-21 school year, CPS began with full remote learning in September 2020, then implemented a phased hybrid return starting with Pre-K and cluster programs in the second quarter. The reopening was contentious, with the Chicago Teachers Union threatening strikes over safety concerns.

schools_affected: 36 schools (ADA accessibility improvements); Multiple schools (roof, envelope, mechanical projects)
description: CPS's FY2021 capital plan totaled $758 million, including $20 million for ADA accessibility improvements at 36 schools as part of a new $100 million, five-year commitment to make all CPS buildings first-floor accessible. Improvements targeted parking lots, main entrances, main offices, and public restrooms. The plan also funded critical facility needs including roof, building envelope, mechanical, electrical, and plumbing repairs, plus full-day Pre-K expansions. CPS estimated it would cost $598 million total to make all schools fully wheelchair accessible. Since FY2016, CPS had invested over $2.1 billion in capital improvements.

schools_affected: 33 schools (ADA accessibility improvements); 750+ active projects district-wide
description: CPS's FY2022 capital plan totaled $706.6 million, including $20.5 million for ADA accessibility at 33 schools, continuing the multi-year $100 million commitment. As of April 2022, over 750 active projects were underway district-wide, prioritizing mechanical systems for indoor air quality, full-day Pre-K expansions, restroom modernizations, student recreation and athletic improvements, and technology upgrades. CPS developed its first Equity Index tool to prioritize resources for schools in greatest need.

schools_affected: All 522 CPS campuses (facilities master plan)
description: CPS released its 2023 Educational Facilities Master Plan, finding that the district would need $14.4 billion to address emergency building repairs and fully modernize all 522 school buildings, with $3 billion in critical needs. The plan determined that 293 of 497 schools (59%) were underutilized (less than 70% capacity), and 163 schools (one-third) were less than half full. The average campus was built in 1940, with 70 facilities dating to before 1900. CPS held 16 neighborhood-specific roundtable discussions from December 2023 through February 2024 to gather community input on priorities for repair, construction, and investment.

schools_affected: No schools closed (moratorium established)
description: In September 2024, a major controversy erupted when the Chicago Teachers Union (CTU) said it obtained a facilities analysis identifying 70 schools that could be consolidated with 70 others, potentially affecting 100+ schools. CPS CEO Pedro Martinez firmly denied closure plans, calling the interpretation false. The CTU House of Delegates passed a vote of no confidence in Martinez. On September 26, 2024, the CPS Board voted unanimously to prohibit any school closures or consolidations through January 2027, extending a state legislative moratorium that was set to expire in January 2025. The district has 61 schools at 30% or less occupancy, compared to 17 at the time of the 2013 mass closures.

schools_affected: Multiple schools (FY2025 capital plan)
description: CPS approved its FY2025 capital plan totaling ~$448 million, including $386.9 million in CPS funding plus $61.5 million in outside funding. Investments include $119.1 million for 15 major roof/envelope projects and 9 mechanical system renovations, $25 million for ADA accessibility at 18 schools, $57 million for programmatic investments (CTE upgrades, library renovations, student recreation/athletics), and continued IT upgrades. The plan builds on the $644.5 million FY2023 capital investment. Since FY2016, CPS has invested over $3.5 billion in capital improvements.

schools_affected: Building 21 (high school in former elementary building); Frankford High School; Mastery Charter Simon Gratz High School; Mitchell Elementary School; C.W. Henry Elementary; Universal Vare Charter School
description: Six Philadelphia schools were abruptly closed between March and May 2023 due to asbestos contamination found in aging buildings. Building 21, in a 100-year-old structure, closed first in March; students relocated to Strawberry Mansion High School. Frankford High (900 students displaced) and others followed in April-May. Previous 1990s sampling had incorrectly labeled some materials as non-asbestos-containing. Asbestos exists in 295 of the district's 329 buildings, with ~80% of schools built before 1978. Board President called the issues "a hundred years in the making" caused by "decades upon decades of disinvestment."

schools_affected: Southwark Elementary School
description: Southwark Elementary became the first school closed in the 2023-24 school year due to asbestos contamination, following the six closures from the prior spring. Students were relocated to South Philadelphia High School. The closure prompted the district to announce a plan for handling future environmental hazard-related closures, including asbestos and flooding, with a commitment to conduct inspections every six months across all facilities.

schools_affected: Frankford High School
description: After nearly two years of closure, Frankford High School reopened on August 18, 2025, following a $29.9 million renovation. The work included asbestos removal and remediation, installation of 6,000 panels to contain remaining fibers, new ceilings with LED lighting, vinyl tile flooring, refinished wood floors, smartboards in every classroom, new windows, and 80+ new air conditioning units. The school welcomed ~1,000 students. In a related development, the district faced federal criminal charges for asbestos regulation violations, the first in the nation, resulting in a deferred prosecution agreement with five years of court monitoring.

schools_affected: 20 schools recommended for closure; 6 schools recommended for co-location/merger; 159 schools recommended for upgrades
description: The School District of Philadelphia released a $2.8 billion Proposed Facilities Master Plan. The plan recommends closing 20 schools (18 in Northeast, Northwest, or West Philadelphia), co-locating or merging 6 schools, and upgrading 159 others, with changes scheduled for the 2027-28 school year. The plan includes $1 billion in district bond funding and requests $1.8 billion in new government/philanthropic funding. Goals include reducing buildings rated Unsatisfactory or Poor from 85 to 0. The district has classroom space for 180,000 students but serves only 116,000. The plan drew immediate opposition from families, educators, and elected officials.

schools_affected: All district schools (capital improvement plan)
description: The district's capital improvement plan allocated $2.489 billion from January 2023 to June 2028, including $602+ million for new construction, $440 million for major renovations, and $353 million for HVAC systems. The district's 300+ buildings average 73 years old, with some dating to 120 years; more than 200 were built before 1978 using lead-based paint and asbestos. Each school is being sorted into five potential outcomes: maintain, modernize, co-locate, repurpose, or close. The district received 8,000 responses to a public survey, with most respondents preferring renovation over closure.

schools_affected: All district schools (settlement agreement)
description: The Philadelphia School District reached a settlement agreement with the city, under which the city committed $2.5 million to help with asbestos and environmental hazard data management and vet an "asbestos investigator workforce." State lawmakers requested $5 billion over five years to address the "facilities crisis," including asbestos and lead-based paint remediation and installation of air conditioning. At a hearing, officials described conditions including crumbling buildings, environmental hazards, and a lack of basic climate control.

schools_affected: Parkview Elementary; Shadowlawn Elementary; Myrtle Grove K-8 Center (reconfigured to K-5)
description: Miami-Dade repurposed three schools for the 2024-25 school year due to declining enrollment. Parkview Elementary was converted to a specialized exceptional student education (ESE) center. Shadowlawn Elementary became an ESE center. Myrtle Grove K-8 was reconfigured to a K-5 elementary, moving 6th-8th graders to Carol City Middle. About 250 students affected.

schools_affected: Poinciana Park Elementary; Country Club Middle
description: Miami-Dade proposed repurposing Poinciana Park Elementary (168 students, enrollment down 45% over five years) and Country Club Middle for the 2025-26 school year. Seven schools in the north region and four in the central region also had boundary changes proposed.

schools_affected: 11 schools across north and central regions
description: Miami-Dade proposed boundary changes to 11 schools for the 2025-26 school year. The majority of proposals pertained to declining enrollment as private alternatives and the state voucher program continued to draw students away. The district projected a loss of about 4,000 students for 2024-25.

schools_affected: Multiple underused school sites
description: The Miami-Dade school board began considering transforming underused school sites into early learning centers. The initiative aims to leverage existing infrastructure to promote fiscal responsibility while addressing the enrollment decline (13,000 fewer students year-over-year by Aug 2025, from 326k to 313k).

schools_affected: All BCPS schools (district-wide)
description: Broward County voters approved an $800 million SMART Bond referendum (Safety, Music, Art, Athletics, Renovations, Technology) with 74% approval. Combined with $184 million in existing capital, the total program reached $984 million. The program addressed up to $3 billion in deferred maintenance including roofing, HVAC, fire systems, ADA compliance, and STEM labs. Program was plagued by mismanagement; a 2021 grand jury report led to Gov. DeSantis removing four board members in 2022. Program officially ended Oct 31, 2025, though 100+ projects continue as capital projects.

schools_affected: Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School
description: An $18 million replacement classroom building opened on the southwest side of the MSD campus, replacing the freshman building where the 2018 mass shooting occurred. The two-story, 45,000 sq ft building replaced the original three-story structure. Students had been learning in portables during construction.

schools_affected: Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School (1200 Building)
description: Demolition of the original building where the 2018 Parkland shooting occurred began on June 14, 2024, and was completed by July 5. The building had been preserved as a crime scene through the trial. Future plans for the site include a possible "legacy field" for sports or band practice.

schools_affected: Broward Estates Elementary (Lauderhill)
description: Phase 1 of the "Redefining Our Schools" initiative closed Broward Estates Elementary, repurposing it as an early learning center. The district also converted four elementary schools into K-8 schools and one middle school into a 6-12 school. This was the first phase of a multi-year plan to address 50,000 empty seats across 300 schools.

schools_affected: Sunshine Elementary (Miramar); Panther Run Elementary (Pembroke Pines); Palm Cove Elementary (Pembroke Pines); North Fork Elementary (Fort Lauderdale); Plantation Middle School; Seagull Alternative High School (Fort Lauderdale)
description: Phase 2 of "Redefining Our Schools" closed six schools. The board voted Jan 21-22, 2026. Sunshine Elementary consolidated into Fairway Elementary. Panther Run students sent to Chapel Trail and Silver Palms. Palm Cove students to Lakeside and Pines Lakes. North Fork consolidated into Croissant Park, MLK Jr., Thurgood Marshall, and Walker elementaries. Plantation Middle merged into Plantation High (becoming 6-12). Seagull consolidated into Whiddon-Rogers. Bair Middle was spared after community advocacy. Estimated savings: $10 million annually. Superintendent said they are "halfway there" to $100 million savings target.

schools_affected: Multiple schools across Broward County
description: Alongside Phase 2 closures, the Broward school board approved boundary changes to redistribute students from closed and consolidated schools. The district identified 68 schools operating at less than 70% capacity. Changes take effect for the 2026-27 school year.

schools_affected: Just Elementary; Cleveland Elementary; Adams Elementary; McLane Middle; Monroe Middle; Kimbell Elementary
description: Hillsborough closed six schools - the first closures due to low enrollment in the district's 140-year history. 24% of schools were overcrowded while 44% were under-enrolled. Kimbell became HOST (after-school care) HQ; McLane became an ESE office; Monroe is used for storage. Just Elementary closure was controversial as the school was 82% Black.

schools_affected: 103 schools with boundary changes; 6 schools repurposed; 3 schools partially repurposed
description: The school board voted 4-3 to approve massive boundary redesign for the 2024-25 school year. The plan impacts roughly 15,000 students (down from an initial proposal affecting 24,000). Boundaries for 103 schools were redrawn. The district hired WXY Studio to review boundaries and address the imbalance of overcrowded and under-enrolled schools. Estimated savings of $13 million.

schools_affected: Just Elementary (rebuild); Stewart Middle Magnet (rebuild)
description: Hillsborough announced plans to rebuild Just Elementary and Stewart Middle Magnet as a combined campus project in west Tampa - the first new schools built in Tampa's urban core in 30 years. Just will accommodate 500 students and Stewart 800. Cost estimated at $70 million (with some estimates reaching higher). Just Elementary is scheduled to reopen August 2027.

schools_affected: Just Elementary (replacement campus); Stewart Middle School (replacement campus); New South County middle school
description: The school board approved nearly $150 million in new construction including replacement campuses for Just/Stewart in Tampa and a new middle school in the South County area. The vote occurred amid concerns about Florida's expanded Schools of Hope program, which could allow charter schools to claim unused space in new buildings that haven't yet reached full enrollment.

schools_affected: All Hillsborough County schools
description: Hillsborough County voters approved a new millage for school operations (Referendum 2) with 66.55% of the vote in November 2024. This provides additional funding for school facilities and operations.

schools_affected: All Polk County schools
description: Polk County voters approved a 15-year renewal of the half-cent sales tax for schools (through Dec 2034). Originally approved in 2003, the tax funds capital projects including new construction, modernization, security, and technology. The tax generates critical revenue for the 7th largest district in Florida (also the 4th lowest funded). A 21-member oversight committee monitors spending.

schools_affected: Scenic Terrace K-8 (new); Elbert Elementary (modernization)
description: A public-private partnership delivered the brand-new Scenic Terrace school in Haines City in just 9 months, on time and on budget. The 157,000 sq ft facility has capacity for 1,600 students. Initially it served as a temporary home for Elbert Elementary students while that school undergoes complete modernization. Scenic Terrace will then become a permanent K-8 school to serve the rapidly growing district.

schools_affected: Lake Region High School (agriculture facility); McLaughlin Academy of Excellence (new gymnasium)
description: Lake Region High School opened a new 2,145 sq ft agriculture facility for ag studies, located near the school's exterior ag area. McLaughlin Academy of Excellence also cut the ribbon on a new gymnasium. Both projects were funded through the half-cent sales tax.

schools_affected: Saddle View Elementary (new)
description: Saddle View Elementary opened Aug 11, 2025, with 631 students in a $41.7 million, 95,990 sq ft facility designed for 971 students. Built to relieve overcrowding at Binks Forest Elementary in the rapidly growing Arden community west of Wellington. Features indoor-outdoor agriculture lab with hydroponic gardens. Opened two years ahead of the original schedule due to rapid growth in western communities.

schools_affected: New elementary school (Westlake area)
description: Palm Beach County is planning a new elementary school estimated at $42.9 million to open in August 2027 in the City of Westlake, which was founded in 2016 and had a population approaching 7,000 by 2024. Saddle View is one of three new schools planned for the western part of the county in the next five years.

schools_affected: 120+ teachers reassigned; 67 schools operating below 70% capacity
description: Declining enrollment forced at least 120 teacher reassignments and threatened $25 million in state funding cuts. Analysis found 67 schools (nearly one-third of the district) operating below 70% capacity. Hardest hit included Indian Pines Elementary (39% full) and Benoist Farms Elementary (41% full). The district explicitly stated it is NOT pursuing closures or consolidations at this time, distinguishing itself from neighboring Broward and Miami-Dade.

schools_affected: 150+ campuses district-wide
description: Duval County voters overwhelmingly approved (67%) a half-penny sales tax to fund $1.9 billion in school repairs and new construction over 15 years. Duval schools are on average the oldest in the state. The tax funds the Master Facility Plan covering renovations, rebuilds, safety/security upgrades, and new construction. Revenue exceeded projections but inflation offset gains. By Nov 2021, revenue reached $92.27 million.

schools_affected: Rutledge Pearson Elementary (new, $28M); Jean Ribault High School (rebuild); Chaffee Trail Middle (rebuild); Highland Elementary (rebuild); Southside Estates Elementary (rebuild)
description: Multiple new school buildings began emerging from the half-penny funded Master Facility Plan. Rutledge Pearson consolidates three schools into one new $28M facility. Jean Ribault High School rebuild (first new high school building since Atlantic Coast opened in 2010) began construction Sept 2023 with anticipated occupancy Aug 2025. Safety and security upgrades in progress at 42 schools.

schools_affected: 18 schools planned for closure over 5 years; 6 new schools to be built
description: The school board approved (6-1) a five-year plan suggesting closure of 18 schools and construction of six new ones. The plan addresses a $1.4 billion budget gap caused by increased post-pandemic construction costs, revenue sharing with charter schools, and shrinking enrollment. Superintendent Bernier noted schools need about 700 students to cover operational costs; about a third of 96 elementary schools meet that threshold.

schools_affected: Annie R. Morgan Elementary (Westside); Kings Trail Elementary (San Jose); Susie E. Tolbert Elementary (NW Jacksonville)
description: The board voted to close three elementary schools at the end of the 2024-25 school year, consolidating students into neighboring schools. Consolidation of Don Brewer and Merrill Road elementaries was delayed after concerns about poor planning. The NAACP raised equity concerns given the district's history with desegregation.

schools_affected: Hyde Grove Elementary (into Hyde Park Elementary); Long Branch Elementary (into R.L. Brown Elementary); Anchor Academy (into Mayport or Atlantic Beach Elementary); Joseph Stilwell Middle (into Ed White, becoming 6-12)
description: Additional schools scheduled for closure/consolidation consideration in the second year of the 5-year Master Facility Plan. The district will provide transportation for students whose new school is more than 1.5 miles from home and may establish bus stops at closed school sites.

schools_affected: Knights Point K-8 (new); Voyager K-8 (new)
description: Osceola County opened two new K-8 schools in 2024, each accommodating about 1,400 students, to address rapid population growth (county grew 46% from 2010 to 2022). The district has over 73,000 students and projects exceeding 100,000 within 10 years. Construction spending increased from $30 million to approximately $1 billion over 3.5 years.

schools_affected: 78 projects across the district
description: The school board detailed hundreds of millions in active projects: 5 in planning, 26 in design, 31 under construction, and 16 in closeout, totaling $919 million. Includes comprehensive renovation of the Osceola County School of the Arts. The district's chief facilities officer noted a dramatic increase from $30 million to nearly $1 billion in construction.

schools_affected: Kindred K-8 School (new, $75M)
description: A $75 million K-8 school is being built along Cross Prairie Parkway in the new Kindred community of Kissimmee. The school was scheduled to open for the 2025-26 school year, adding capacity for approximately 1,400 students in one of Florida's fastest-growing areas.

schools_affected: Reedy Creek Elementary (rebuild, $59M)
description: Osceola County Schools broke ground on a $59 million rebuild of Reedy Creek Elementary, split into two phases. The project is part of the district's effort to manage explosive growth in the county.

schools_affected: New high school ($184M)
description: A new high school with an $184 million construction budget funded through county impact fees will open for the 2026 school year. It will include 11 permanent buildings for 2,522 students - the first high school built since Tohopekaliga High School opened in 2018.

schools_affected: Cross Bayou Elementary (closure); Disston Academy (closure); Bay Point Elementary + Bay Point Middle (consolidation to K-8); Oldsmar Elementary (expansion to K-8)
description: Superintendent Kevin Hendrick recommended closing Cross Bayou Elementary and Disston Academy at the end of 2025-26, creating a K-8 school combining Bay Point Elementary and Bay Point Middle on the middle school campus in 2027-28, and expanding Oldsmar Elementary to K-8 in 2026-27. The district has 35,000 more seats than students and about a third of campuses sit below 60% capacity. Estimated savings: $8 million annually. A larger round of closures is expected next fall.

schools_affected: Fort Myers Beach Elementary; Hector A. Cafferata Jr. Elementary; The Sanibel School; 11 schools total with significant damage
description: Hurricane Ian (Sept 2022) caused an estimated $230-$300 million in damage to Lee County schools. Fort Myers Beach Elementary (built 1947, on the National Register) and Cafferata Elementary suffered the worst damage. Cafferata's 715 students were split between two temporary locations. The Sanibel School also sustained major damage.

schools_affected: District-wide recovery projects
description: The School District of Lee County received $51 million in Hurricane Ian recovery funds as part of a $338 million total award to Lee County agencies. This was the highest allocation to a single entity, tied only with the City of Cape Coral. The district also received a $55 million loan from Florida's Department of Emergency Management. HUD awarded Lee County $1.1 billion total for long-term recovery.

schools_affected: Hector A. Cafferata Jr. Elementary K-8 (new build)
description: A brand-new Cafferata K-8 school was planned to open during the 2024-25 school year on district-owned property in Cape Coral, replacing the original elementary school destroyed by Hurricane Ian. The new school expands to serve middle school grades as well.

schools_affected: Fort Myers Beach Elementary (closed again)
description: Fort Myers Beach Elementary, which had been in recovery from Hurricane Ian, was closed again after Hurricanes Helene and Milton (Sept-Oct 2024) caused significant flood damage. Students were relocated to San Carlos Park Elementary. The district is now considering five repair/rebuild options ranging from $1.3M to $15.9M. FEMA awarded $11.4M for the school. A final decision on the school's future is expected June 2025.

schools_affected: Lake Mary Elementary (replacement, $24M)
description: Seminole County Public Schools announced plans to build a $24 million replacement of Lake Mary Elementary School at 132 S. Country Club Road, Lake Mary. The district sought a construction manager at risk for the project. Seminole County is the #1 rated public school district in Florida by Niche, with 94% of schools rated A or B.

schools_affected: Hundreds of underenrolled schools across Florida
description: Florida expanded the Schools of Hope law, allowing for-profit charter schools to claim classroom space in under-capacity public schools for free ("co-location"). Charter operator Mater Academy sent letters to ~90 public schools; Academica sent hundreds of letters. Districts including Hillsborough, Pinellas, Orange, and Duval flagged dozens of schools as vulnerable. This law is accelerating closure/consolidation decisions in many districts. Proposed rule changes in Feb 2026 would limit charters to schools below 75% capacity or with 400+ open seats.

schools_affected: 5 new schools; 7 school renovations
description: Wake County voters approved a $530.7 million school bond referendum on November 8, 2022, as part of over $1 billion in bond approvals. The bond funds construction of five new schools (elementary schools in Apex, Fuquay-Varina, and Wendell; a middle school in Morrisville; and a high school serving west Cary/Morrisville) plus major renovations at seven existing schools. Property tax impact was 1 cent per $100 of assessed value. The bond supplements a 7-year building plan (FY 2023-2029) totaling $2.632 billion for 11 new schools and 10 major renovations.

schools_affected: Bowling Road Elementary (Fuquay-Varina); Pleasant Plains Elementary (Apex); Rex Road Elementary (Holly Springs); Felton Grove High School (Apex)
description: Four new schools opened for the 2025-26 school year to address tremendous growth in Southern Wake County. Rex Road Elementary is a 133,000 sq ft campus designed for 800 K-5 students. The four new schools bring the district total to 203 schools serving 161,115+ students. The district forecasts growth to 170,000+ students over the next 10 years, with five more schools planned in that period. In 2021-22, 11% of teaching spaces were in 894 mobile/modular classrooms.

schools_affected: Morrisville High School (Little/Davis Drive site)
description: Morrisville High School is planned to open for the 2027-2028 school year with students in grades 9-10. Prior to that, Wake Early College of Information and Biotechnologies will occupy a portion of the building beginning as early as November 2025. A Parkside Middle School is planned to open no earlier than the 2028-2029 school year.

schools_affected: 30 bond projects across the district
description: Mecklenburg County voters approved a historic $2.5 billion school bond, the largest school bond in North Carolina history. The bond covers 30 projects including new middle schools in Huntersville, south and southwest Charlotte; a new health-sciences magnet high school in uptown Charlotte; a new regional athletic facility in west Charlotte; and 25 renovation and replacement projects. Funded by a 3-cent property tax increase phased in during 2025, 2028, and 2029. As enrollment growth slows, the bond shifts focus from new construction to replacing existing aging schools.

schools_affected: Billingsville Elementary (renovation); Sedgefield Elementary (renovation to Montessori magnet); Marie G. Davis School (renovation to Montessori 7-12 magnet)
description: The first projects from the 2023 $2.5 billion bond were completed by August 2025. Billingsville and Sedgefield elementaries and Marie G. Davis School were renovated and reopened as Montessori magnet schools, replacing the older Chantilly, Park Road, and J.T. Williams buildings. Sedgefield moved pre-K-2 students into the Dilworth building in August 2024 as part of the transition.

schools_affected: South Mecklenburg High School (replacement of 1958 building)
description: South Mecklenburg High School replacement of a 1958 classroom building is scheduled for completion in August 2027, funded with both 2017 and 2023 bonds. The replacement of North Mecklenburg High School (opened 1951) is the most expensive project at approximately $228.5 million, scheduled for 2028-2030.

schools_affected: New middle school (Stumptown Road, Huntersville)
description: A new middle school on Stumptown Road in Huntersville is scheduled for completion in August 2028. It will relieve crowding in northern schools, allow the district to add magnet seats, and absorb students from Davidson K-8 when that school converts to an elementary school. CMS is also converting several schools: Thomasboro PreK-8 becomes elementary only, University Park Creative Arts becomes a full K-5 arts magnet, and Rea Farms STEAM becomes a full K-8 magnet.

schools_affected: 7 elementary school renovations; 8 elementary school designs; 1 middle school design; 25+ schools (security vestibules)
description: Fairfax County voters approved a $435 million school bond referendum with 67% support on November 7, 2023. Funds support renovation of seven elementary schools, planning/design of eight additional elementary schools and one middle school, three modular relocations, and security vestibule installation at 25+ schools. FCPS maintains a triple-A bond rating, saving taxpayers an estimated $1 billion in financing costs. School facilities are valued at nearly $6.5 billion.

schools_affected: Braddock Elementary; Louise Archer Elementary; Crossfield Elementary; Mosby Woods Elementary; Bonnie Brae Elementary; Cooper Middle School; Falls Church High School
description: Major renovation projects continued across FCPS as part of the FY 2025-29 CIP. Braddock Elementary ($35.6M) and Louise Archer Elementary ($29.4M) renovations were completed. Crossfield, Mosby Woods, and Bonnie Brae elementaries completed or neared completion. Cooper Middle School and Falls Church High School renovations were underway. FCPS operates on a 41-year renovation cycle for its facilities.

schools_affected: Dunn Loring Elementary (new, from administrative center); Silver Line Elementary (new); Western High School (acquisition and renovation)
description: The FY 2027-2031 CIP requires $1.1 billion over five years for renovation, maintenance, and construction. Plans include repurposing the Dunn Loring Administrative Center into a new elementary school to relieve overcrowding in the Dunn Loring/Falls Church/Tysons area, constructing a new Silver Line Elementary, and acquiring and renovating Western High School. Enrollment is expected to decline from ~177,000 to ~171,000 by 2030-31.

schools_affected: Woodbridge Area Elementary School (new)
description: A new elementary school in the Woodbridge area opened for the 2025-26 school year. The district's CIP 2025-2030 was reassessed based on projected enrollment declines, with several projects slated for delay including the 14th high school and Brentsville District High School renovations.

schools_affected: 14th High School (cancelled)
description: Prince William County officially cancelled plans for its 14th high school, which had been delayed multiple times due to declining enrollment. PWCS data showed the county anticipates 1,030 vacant seats across existing 13 high schools by 2029. The district projects a decrease of approximately 3,776 students over the next five years. Northern Virginia experienced its first population decline since 1970, as residents move to Richmond and exurbs due to housing costs and remote work.

schools_affected: 162 school buildings over 25 years old; 40 HVAC systems not functioning properly
description: MCPS unveiled its "Hard Truths About Our School Buildings" presentation, revealing that nearly two-thirds of its 238 school buildings (162 buildings) are more than 25 years old, with $740 million in overdue projects including 40 non-functioning HVAC systems. The district needs $175 million to replace roofs older than 20 years. To reach long-term goals, MCPS would need to renovate 6-7 elementary schools and 3 middle/high schools every year for 20 years; currently averaging only 5 schools per year.

schools_affected: 13 Major Capital Projects (4 HS, 2 MS, 7 ES)
description: The Board of Education accepted a $2.78 billion Capital Improvements Program (FY 2027-2032) targeting aging buildings, critical systems, and infrastructure. Includes 13 Major Capital Projects (four high schools, two middle schools, seven elementary schools) for completion within six years, plus $521.4 million for HVAC/roof replacements and $303.8 million for other infrastructure renewal. County Executive Marc Elrich proposed $2.1 billion for MCPS in the county's $6.6 billion CIP -- a record allocation.

schools_affected: Crown High School (Gaithersburg, new); Charles W. Woodward High School (reopening)
description: Crown High School in Gaithersburg is expected to open in 2027, along with the reopening of Charles W. Woodward High School and an expansion of Damascus High School for the 2027-2028 year. Parents raised concerns about plans to initially use Crown as a "holding school." The openings require comprehensive boundary studies with at least seven options being considered for attendance zone redraws.

schools_affected: Silver Spring International Middle School (proposed closure 2030)
description: The MCPS superintendent proposed closing the 90-year-old Silver Spring International Middle School in 2030 and converting it to a holding school. In December 2025, the school board suspended consideration of the closure, choosing to incorporate the decision into a future holistic study of elementary school boundaries. Enrollment has dropped to a 10-year low, with steeper declines projected due to lower birth rates and fewer international students. The district has not shuttered a campus in decades.

schools_affected: 8 new schools (6 elementary, 2 K-8)
description: PGCPS brought more than $660 million in taxable sustainable revenue bonds to fast-track construction of eight new schools via a public-private partnership (P3) -- the second P3 package for the district but the first using taxable municipal bonds. The eight schools (six elementary and two K-8) comprise 1.03 million sq ft with enrolling capacity of approximately 8,150 students. Prince George's County contributes $69 million annually to the P3 fund.

schools_affected: Eutaw-Marshburn Elementary (West Baltimore); Steuart Hill Academic Academy (Union Square); New Era Academy (South Baltimore)
description: The Baltimore City school board voted to permanently close three public schools during summer 2023, citing low enrollment and deteriorating buildings. A fourth school, Dr. Bernard Harris Elementary, was kept open as its facility issues were less severe. The board also voted unanimously to develop a strategic plan for long-term enrollment and school closures.

schools_affected: Baltimore City College; Frederick Douglass High School; Baltimore Polytechnic Institute; Western High School
description: Baltimore City invested $400 million in renovating its oldest school buildings as part of the 21st Century School Buildings Program successor (Built to Learn Act of 2021). Baltimore City College moved to the former Thurgood Marshall HS building for three years during construction. Frederick Douglass HS moved to Garrison Middle for two years. Polytechnic Institute and Western High were slated to move in 2025 to Northwestern and Chinquapin buildings respectively. The program has delivered 29 new or renovated schools at approximately $40 million each.

schools_affected: Lansdowne High School (new, $26M state funds); Towson High School (renovation, $20M state funds); Deer Park Elementary (new, $15M state funds); Scott's Branch Elementary (new, $10M state funds); Dundalk High School (addition, $8M state funds); Pine Grove Middle School (addition, $1M state funds)
description: Baltimore County received $80 million in additional state grant funds to accelerate major school construction projects. These are part of County Executive Olszewski's $3.3 billion plan to improve every school in Baltimore County over 15 years, including almost $210 million in new spending in 2023. Just under 80% of BCPS school buildings are 40+ years old. The Multi-Year Improvement Plan for All Schools (MYIPAS) was commissioned in 2020 using CannonDesign consultants.

schools_affected: Campfield Early Learning Center (Gwynn Oak)
description: The Baltimore County Board of Education voted on March 11, 2025 to close Campfield Early Learning Center at the end of the current academic year, earlier than the originally planned 2025-26 closure. With fewer than 60 students projected, officials determined students' needs could be better met at home schools or nearby regional programs. The Campfield site was approved in January 2024 as the future location of the Northwest Area Career and Technology Education Center. The original closure was approved by a 6-5 board vote in September 2023.

schools_affected: All GCPS schools (district-wide E-SPLOST continuation)
description: Gwinnett County voters approved continuation of the existing E-SPLOST (Education Special Purpose Local Option Sales Tax) with 76.6% support. Since 1997, E-SPLOST has funded construction of 64 new schools and 101 school additions, plus technology upgrades and classroom modernization. GCPS holds a "Aaa" bond rating from both Moody's and S&P -- one of only two Georgia school districts to do so.

schools_affected: Seckinger High School (new); Jones Middle School (two-story addition)
description: Seckinger High School opened as the biggest highlight of GCPS new facilities for fall 2022. Jones Middle School received a new two-story addition. Both projects were funded by voter-approved E-SPLOST sales tax and bonds from the 2018 GO Bond referendum ($350 million, approved with 78% support), which also funded general building renovations, safety enhancements, and technology upgrades district-wide.

schools_affected: Archer High School (three-story addition); Berkmar High School (cafeteria renovation); North Gwinnett High School (25-classroom addition); Trickum Middle School (25-classroom addition); 13 career and technical lab projects
description: Major summer 2025 construction included a three-story addition at Archer High and cafeteria renovation at Berkmar High. HVAC systems were replaced at seven schools (Bethesda ES, Camp Creek ES, Collins Hill HS, Crews MS, Creekland MS, Harris ES, Northbrook/Buice Centers). 13 career/tech lab projects were completed at Brookwood HS, Archer HS, Dacula HS, Parkview HS, Pinckneyville MS, Shiloh MS, and Maxwell HS of Technology. Murphy Middle School and a 20-classroom wing at Harbins Elementary open August 2026.

schools_affected: Pope High School (facility upgrades); Sprayberry High School (stadium improvements); South Cobb High School (stadium improvements)
description: Ed-SPLOST VI-funded renovations across the district include Pope High School receiving front entry improvements, new flooring, locker removal, and substantial athletic facility upgrades (renovated locker rooms, new baseball restroom/concessions building, field improvements) with completion expected November 2025. Sprayberry and South Cobb High Schools received upgraded grandstands and ADA-compliant stadium improvements by May 2025. Cobb Schools avoids bond financing entirely, relying on Ed-SPLOST's one-penny sales tax and maintaining three Triple-A credit ratings.

schools_affected: District-wide (138 schools)
description: DeKalb County unveiled a "reimagining" plan (student assignment planning) to serve as a roadmap for the next decade. The plan recommended redistricting throughout the county by 2030, consolidation of some elementary schools, creation of K-8 facilities in some areas, and rebuilding other schools with sales tax funds. The district declined from 100,000+ students in 2016 to about 92,000, leaving many buildings under-utilized. The process is expected to take 18 months to two years.

schools_affected: Idlewood Elementary; Austin Elementary (new facility); Dunwoody Cluster elementary schools
description: The Board of Education approved redistricting for Idlewood Elementary on February 10, 2025. A separate redistricting process determined new attendance lines for a new Austin Elementary facility to better balance enrollment across Dunwoody Cluster elementary schools. An earlier process had established lines for a new elementary school in Doraville for the 2020-21 school year to balance enrollment in Chamblee and Cross Keys clusters.

schools_affected: Spalding Drive Charter Elementary (Sandy Springs, opened 1966); Parklane Elementary (East Point, opened 1953)
description: The Fulton County School Board voted on February 20, 2025 to approve closure and redistricting of Spalding Drive Charter Elementary and Parklane Elementary due to the cost of operations, declining enrollment, and aging buildings. Community forums were held in fall 2024 to explain rationale and draw potential new attendance zones for surrounding schools. The closures and new redistricting plan take effect in the 2025-26 school year. FCS is now one of the only metro Atlanta districts free of bond debt, having made its final bond payment, and relies on SPLOST for construction.

schools_affected: Denver Discovery School; Fairview Elementary School; Math and Science Leadership Academy
description: Denver's school board voted to close three schools at the end of the 2022-23 school year after a contentious process that initially proposed 10 closures. The three schools had "critically low enrollment." Of the closed buildings, two were in shared buildings still occupied by other schools; Fairview Elementary was repurposed as a special education program (Next Steps by Chancelight). Enrollment had declined from 86,949 in 2019 to 82,997 in 2022.

schools_affected: 7 schools closed; 3 schools partially closed (grade restructure)
description: The Denver school board voted to shutter seven schools and shrink three more at the end of the 2024-25 school year. The closures eliminate nearly 4,000 vacant seats and save $6.6 million annually. The changes affect 1,087 students (~1% of ~90,000 enrollment). Students of color and low-income families are disproportionately impacted -- seven of 10 schools serve higher percentages of students of color than the district average. Partial closures: Kunsmiller Creative Arts Academy loses elementary grades; Dora Moore ECE-8 loses middle school grades; Denver Center for International Studies loses high school grades.

schools_affected: Palmer Elementary (converted to preschool center); Columbian Elementary (reuse pending); 3 other closed buildings (reuse pending)
description: Denver Public Schools announced repurposing plans for closed elementary buildings. Palmer Elementary at 995 Grape St. will become a preschool center for 2025-26, expanding from three to four preschool classrooms. Plans for Columbian Elementary and other closed buildings remain undetermined. Repurposing funds come from a separate bond measure Denver voters approved in 2024 earmarked for school reconfigurations. The district is managing multiple vacant properties, including Rosedale Elementary (leased to Catholic Archdiocese in 2021, now St. John Paul the Great HS).

schools_affected: 2 new elementary schools (RidgeGate and Sterling Ranch); Sierra Middle School (expansion); All schools (safety/security updates)
description: Douglas County voters approved a $490 million bond (Ballot Issue 5A) with 59% support -- after rejecting a bond request in 2023. The bond allocates $150 million for new school construction in RidgeGate and Sterling Ranch and expansion of Sierra Middle School; $178.9 million for capital renewal and replacement; and $38.2 million for career and technical education (CTE) programs. No property tax increase required -- the district will restructure debt to maintain the current 5.2 mill tax rate. This is the seventh bond since 1984, and the largest since a $250 million package in 2018. More than 62,000 students attend 90 schools.

schools_affected: Emory Elementary; Peck Elementary; Thomson Elementary; Campbell Elementary; Peiffer Elementary; Colorow Elementary; Green Mountain Elementary; Bergen Meadow K-2; Molholm Elementary; Glennon Heights Elementary; Parr Elementary; Sheridan Green Elementary; Witt Elementary; Vivian Elementary; Wilmore Davis Elementary; Kullerstrand Elementary
description: The Jeffco Board of Education voted unanimously on November 10, 2022 to close 16 elementary schools -- the largest mass closure in the district's history. Enrollment dropped from 87,700 in 2000 to 77,205 by fall 2022, with capacity for 96,000 students across 157 schools. The closures affected 2,400+ children and 422 full-time employees. The district faced a budget deficit and had drawn $32 million from reserves. Closures were expected to save up to $12 million annually. Criteria required enrollment below 220 students or capacity utilization below 45%.

schools_affected: Coal Creek Canyon K-8; Arvada K-8; Moore Middle School (consolidated with Pomona HS to become Jr/Sr HS)
description: The school board voted to close two additional K-8 schools and consolidate a middle school, bringing total closures to 21 since 2021. Coal Creek Canyon K-8 was the lowest-enrolled school with fewer than 85 students (45% decline since 2019). Arvada K-8 used only 60% capacity with fewer than 560 students. Moore Middle was consolidated with Pomona High to create Pomona Jr/Sr High (grades 6-12). Jefferson Academy was authorized to open a replication site in the Coal Creek Canyon building.

schools_affected: Jefferson Jr./Sr. High School (Edgewater, proposed transition)
description: Jeffco began considering closing Jefferson Jr./Sr. High School (grades 7-12) and converting it into a specialized career-focused high school. A boundary study found the school unsustainable with projected enrollment of only 372 students by 2027-28 -- with 47% of boundary families already choosing other schools. The district frames it as a "transition" rather than closure, though board members noted it "sounds a lot like closing a school." The district manages 22 closed school properties, with maintenance costing ~$150,000 per year per building. Eight properties found new owners; 14 remain unsold.

schools_affected: 20 new schools built; 37 classroom additions; 18 replacement schools; 82 modernization projects
description: By mid-2021, the 2015 Capital Improvement Program (authorized through Senate Bills 119 and 207) had completed or begun dozens of projects including 20 new schools, 37 classroom additions, 18 replacement schools, five phased replacement schools, and 82 modernization projects. The original 10-year program estimated at $4.1 billion was later extended through 2035 by the state Legislature. The school board gave final approval for $3.5 billion in facility projects for the next 14 years.

schools_affected: 10 schools (construction paused); 125 aging facilities under review
description: CCSD Trustees voted unanimously to pause construction on 10 schools for one year due to project bids increasing 60% and material costs rising 40%. Paused projects include Indian Springs and Cashman Middle School, Northwest Comprehensive High School, and Southeast Choice High School. The district has 125 schools classified as "aging facilities" and projects losing 3,600 students annually. The district needs $15.3 billion in capital bonds but has only $7.3 billion available. CannonDesign was hired for $5 million to assess all school facilities. A Facility Master Plan with closure/reuse recommendations is expected in early 2026.

district_name: Nevada State Public Charter School Authority
schools_affected: 6 CCSD charter schools absorbed; 5 new charter schools opening 2025-26; 80 charter school campuses statewide
description: The SPCSA expanded significantly, absorbing six Clark County School District-run charter schools in January 2025 (marking CCSD's complete exit from charter school operation) and planning five new charter school openings for 2025-26. Total enrollment surpassed the Washoe County School District, reaching ~69,000 students with projections above 70,000. The expansion adds over 8,000 students, positioning SPCSA as Nevada's second-largest local education agency. 79% of new campuses opened in the last five years are Title I schools. SPCSA schools have an 83.3% graduation rate, with 26 of 27 high schools exceeding the statewide rate.

district_name: Nevada State Public Charter School Authority
schools_affected: All Nevada public schools including charters
description: The Nevada Legislature passed SB500 securing $12.9 billion for K-12 funding (2025-27 biennium), providing historic investment levels. AB398 allocated $128 million for teacher raises including charter school teachers (previously excluded). SB468 allocated $7 million for charter school student transportation. Cities of Henderson and North Las Vegas were approved as new charter school authorizers under Gov. Lombardo's Assembly Bill 400, allowing municipalities to sponsor and oversee charter schools within their boundaries.

title: TEA State Takeover
schools_affected: All 270+ HISD campuses
description: TEA formally took over Houston ISD, replacing the elected school board with an appointed Board of Managers and installing Mike Miles (former Dallas ISD superintendent) as superintendent. The takeover was triggered by Wheatley High School receiving five consecutive F ratings under state accountability. At the time, HISD had a B+ accountability rating overall and a AAA bond rating.

title: New Education System (NES) -- Phase 1 Restructuring
schools_affected: 28 campuses in Wheatley, Kashmere, and North Forest HS feeder patterns (including Kashmere HS, Wheatley HS, North Forest HS, Highland Heights ES, Henry MS, Sugar Grove Academy, Marshall ES, and others)
description: Superintendent Miles launched the NES at 28 historically underperforming campuses. All staff were required to reapply for positions. Schools adopted extended 6:30 AM to 5 PM schedules, new curricula, and centralized budget management. Libraries were converted to "TEAMS centers." An additional 57 schools voluntarily joined as "NES-Aligned" campuses.

title: NES Expansion -- Phase 2
schools_affected: 45 additional campuses (including Austin High School and 18 elementary/middle schools), bringing total to 130 NES campuses
description: HISD expanded NES to 45 more schools, 26 of which were required to join based on failing state ratings and 19 that joined voluntarily. This brought the total NES footprint to 130 campuses -- nearly half the district.

title: $4.4 Billion Bond Rejected
schools_affected: District-wide (would have funded repairs/rebuilds across all campuses)
description: Houston voters overwhelmingly rejected HISD's $4.4 billion bond proposal (Prop A: $3.96B for facilities; Prop B: $440M for technology) by a 58-42% margin. It was the largest school bond in Texas history and the first $1B+ Texas school bond to fail. Both Democratic and Republican parties opposed it under the slogan "No Trust, No Bond," viewing it as a referendum on the state-appointed leadership. Miles estimated the district needs $10B in repairs.

title: School Closures Proposed Then Reversed
schools_affected: Up to 10 unspecified "small" campuses
description: At convocation, Miles announced he would propose closing up to 10 small schools due to declining enrollment (30,000 students lost in 10 years). Each closure would save approximately $2M/year. However, in November 2025, the district reversed course and announced no closures for the 2026-27 school year, though "consolidations" may be considered later.

title: TEA Takeover Extended to 2027
schools_affected: District-wide
description: TEA Commissioner Mike Morath extended state control of HISD until at least June 1, 2027. Three criteria must be met for a return to local control: no campuses failing for multiple consecutive years, special education compliance, and the board demonstrating proper governance.

title: $100M Infrastructure Spending from General Fund
schools_affected: District-wide
description: After the bond failure, HISD announced it would budget $100 million from its general fund for building updates and infrastructure over two years, reducing funds available for salaries and operations. The district faces a projected $250M budget deficit.

title: $3.47 Billion Bond Approved
schools_affected: 200+ campuses
description: Voters approved Proposition A ($3.2B for school construction, renovation, and equipment at 200+ of 230 campuses) and Proposition B ($270M for technology). Three other propositions for sports stadiums, performing arts, and swimming pools were rejected. The bond funds 14 new or replacement campuses.

title: Geneva Heights Elementary Replacement Campus
schools_affected: Geneva Heights Elementary
description: A $31 million replacement campus for Geneva Heights Elementary, with a capacity of 750 students, was constructed as part of the 2020 bond program. It retained a portion of the original building.

title: Three New Schools Opened
schools_affected: Three new campuses (including replacements)
description: Dallas ISD opened the doors of three new schools funded by the 2020 bond program, marking a milestone in the district's facilities transformation.

title: John Quincy Adams and George Peabody Elementary Dedications
schools_affected: John Quincy Adams Elementary, George Peabody Elementary
description: Two replacement campuses -- John Quincy Adams Elementary (unveiled Nov. 14, 2024) and George Peabody Elementary (dedicated Nov. 13, 2024) -- opened as state-of-the-art facilities funded by the 2020 bond.

title: John Lewis Social Justice Academy at O.W. Holmes
schools_affected: O.W. Holmes campus (Southern Dallas)
description: An $80 million investment for the first new campus built in the southern Dallas community in years, part of the 2020 bond addressing historical inequities.

title: Proposed $6.2 Billion Bond for 2026
schools_affected: District-wide; would rebuild 26 campuses and consolidate 2 pairs of schools
description: Dallas ISD staff presented a preliminary $6.2B bond plan for 2026 covering replacement of 26 schools, technology/security upgrades, 500 new buses, and consolidation of Piedmont G.L.O.B.A.L. Academy with San Jacinto ES, and Dr. Frederick Douglass Todd Sr. MS with Whitney M. Young Jr. ES. A Citizens Bond Steering Committee was formed in February 2025.

title: Board Redistricting (Trustee Districts)
schools_affected: District governance
description: Following 2020 Census data, Dallas ISD redrew its Single Member District (trustee) boundaries, holding 35+ community meetings and two TeleTown Halls. The new map was used for the May 2024 elections.

title: $1.2 Billion Bond Narrowly Approved
schools_affected: All middle schools + 4 new elementary schools
description: Proposition A ($1.211B) for school construction and renovation passed by just 42 votes (12,342 to 12,300). It funds major interior renovations to all middle schools and construction of four new elementary schools. Propositions B (Fine Arts, $98.3M), C (Stadiums, $104.9M), and D (Recreation, $76.2M) all failed.

title: Forest Oak Sixth Grade Closed
schools_affected: Forest Oak Sixth Grade
description: Closed due to struggling academic outcomes and state accountability concerns. Forest Oak had earned five consecutive F ratings, putting the district at risk of TEA intervention.

title: Wedgwood Sixth Grade Closed
schools_affected: Wedgwood Sixth Grade
description: Closed due to declining enrollment and underutilization.

title: S.S. Dillow and Eastern Hills Elementary Closures Approved
schools_affected: S.S. Dillow Elementary, Eastern Hills Elementary
description: Board approved closure of both campuses due to declining enrollment and underutilization.

date: August 2024 (McLean approved); December 2024 (West Handley rezoning approved, closes by 2028)
title: McLean 6th Grade and West Handley Elementary Closures
schools_affected: McLean Sixth Grade Center, West Handley Elementary
description: McLean 6th Grade approved for closure in August. West Handley Elementary was effectively closed through an attendance boundary rezoning vote in December.

title: 18-Campus Five-Year Closure Plan Approved
schools_affected: 18 campuses total (4 previously approved + 14 new), including Kirkpatrick ES, H.V. Helbing ES, Riverside Applied Learning Center, Charles E. Nash ES, Atwood McDonald ES, Sunrise-McMillan ES, A.M. Pate ES, Harlean Beal ES, Morningside MS, Edward J. Briscoe ES, Hubbard Heights ES, J.T. Stevens ES, De Zavala ES, and Kirkpatrick MS
description: The board unanimously approved a five-year plan to close 18 campuses (15 elementary, 1 sixth-grade center, 2 middle schools), saving $77.3 million. Closures begin June 2025 and run through June 2029. Community opposition was strong, with 100+ parents packing the meeting. Notably, De Zavala ES had an A rating from TEA.

title: Western Hills Primary Closure
schools_affected: Western Hills Primary (consolidating with Western Hills Elementary)
description: Board voted to consolidate Western Hills Primary with Western Hills Elementary on the same property for the 2026-27 school year. Attendance zones will not change.

title: Bond-Funded Middle School Renovations
schools_affected: 7 middle schools including Wedgwood MS ($46.8M) and Meadowbrook MS ($36.8M)
description: The board approved over $223.5 million in construction contracts for seven middle school renovations as part of the 2021 bond program. Projects include new secured entry vestibules, upgraded corridors, science labs, and removal of portable buildings.

title: $1.76 Billion Bond (Approved 2019, Projects 2020--2024)
schools_affected: District-wide (new schools, renovations, technology, transportation)
description: Voters approved $1.76B for new school construction ($238M technology, $968M facility renovations, $88M transportation). The bond funded the opening of several new campuses through 2024.

title: Rowe Middle School Opened
schools_affected: Rowe Middle School (new campus)
description: New middle school opened as part of the 2019 bond program.

title: Fiest Elementary Renovated
schools_affected: Fiest Elementary School
description: Ribbon-cutting ceremony on Aug. 16, 2021 for the newly renovated campus, part of the 2019 bond's Phase 1 renovations.

title: Dr. Carla Brosnahan Elementary (ES #58) Opened
schools_affected: Dr. Carla Brosnahan Elementary School (Elementary #58)
description: New $33.2 million elementary school opened at 20220 Clay Road in Katy for the 2023-24 school year.

title: Roy J. Sprague Jr. Middle School (MS #20) Opened
schools_affected: Sprague Middle School (Middle School #20)
description: New $66.9 million three-story middle school opened at 10611 Mason Road in the educational village housing Bridgeland High School and Wells Elementary. Named after a 26-year CFISD veteran.

title: Elementary School #59 (Miramesa) Opened
schools_affected: Elementary #59 (in Miramesa subdivision)
description: New elementary school opened at West Road and Miramesa Drive, designed with connected library and cafeteria. This was the final new school in the 2019 bond program.

title: Major Redistricting Affecting 44 Campuses
schools_affected: Up to 44 campuses, including Cypress Ranch HS, Cypress Falls HS, Bridgeland HS, Langham Creek HS, and dozens of elementary/middle schools
description: Board approved sweeping attendance boundary changes in a contentious 4-3 vote to populate three new campuses and relieve overcrowding (Smith MS at 134% capacity, multiple elementary schools at 118%). Over 5,500 community feedback forms were submitted. The Stone Gate neighborhood controversy over the Cypress Ranch-to-Cypress Falls shift was particularly heated.

title: New Administration Building and Transportation Center
schools_affected: District operations
description: Mark Henry, Ed.D. Administration Building (MHAB) opened in 2023, named after the retiring superintendent. Transportation Center #6 opened near Cypress Woods HS for $26.8M, including bus parking, fueling, and training facilities.

title: Kallison Ranch Area Middle School Opened
schools_affected: Kallison Ranch Area Middle School (new campus)
description: $57 million new middle school opened in fall 2021, funded by the 2018 bond ($848.9M). Located in the rapidly growing far west Bexar County area.

title: Village at WestPointe North Elementary Opened
schools_affected: Village at WestPointe North Area Elementary (new campus)
description: $35 million new elementary school opened in fall 2021, funded by the 2018 bond. Serving growth in the WestPointe master-planned community.

title: Sonia M. Sotomayor High School Opened
schools_affected: Sotomayor High School (NISD's 12th high school)
description: $152.5 million new high school (the Galm Area HS project) opened, named after Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor. It is the 12th and newest high school in the district. Opened without a senior class.

title: $992 Million Bond Approved
schools_affected: 81 elementary schools (renovations), 1 new elementary school, district-wide infrastructure
description: NISD voters approved a record $992M bond. A major shift from prior growth-focused bonds: $645.5M went to renovations at 81 elementary schools (classrooms, CTE, fine arts, athletics, libraries, playgrounds); $207.3M for infrastructure upgrades; $45M for one new elementary school (Village at WestPointe West area); $23.7M for a baseball/softball complex near Sotomayor HS.

title: FM 471 North Area Elementary (#4) Opened
schools_affected: New elementary school (FM 471 North area)
description: $35.8 million new elementary school, the last new school funded by the 2018 bond, opened in fall 2023.

title: Chumbley Elementary Opened + Boundary Changes
schools_affected: Chumbley Elementary (new), Cole Elementary, Galm Elementary
description: New $45M elementary school (funded by 2022 bond) opened in far west Bexar County in the Riverstone at WestPointe subdivision. Named "Chumbley Elementary." Boundary changes approved Nov. 14, 2023, affecting Cole ES and Galm ES to populate the new school and relieve overcrowding at Cole.

title: Colonies North Elementary Renovation
schools_affected: Colonies North Elementary
description: $35 million renovation to replace the cafeteria, gymnasium, and several classrooms at this aging campus, funded by the 2022 bond. Board approved the design in December 2023.

title: School Board Redistricting
schools_affected: Governance (7 single-member trustee districts)
description: NISD trustees adopted a new map for single-member trustee districts after 2020 Census data showed a 77.5% population differential between the most and least populous districts (far exceeding the 10% threshold). The new map reduced the differential to 6.7%.

title: $1.26 Billion Bond Approved
schools_affected: District-wide (new schools, renovations, technology, natatorium)
description: All three propositions passed: Prop A (65.66%), Prop B (66.62%), Prop C (56.67%). Funds construction of new schools, safety/security improvements, technology upgrades, and a natatorium. Includes a $223M rebuild of Clements High School (foundation had shifted) and a new elementary school in Harvest Green.

title: Bond Program $165 Million Shortfall
schools_affected: Harvest Green ES (eliminated), transportation facility (deferred), fine arts/athletics projects (reduced)
description: Shortly after projects began, a $165M deficit was discovered in the $1.26B bond program. Investigation showed district leaders failed to adjust costs for inflation when the bond was delayed from Nov 2022 to May 2023. On Oct. 21, 2024, trustees voted to eliminate the new Harvest Green elementary school ($47.6M), defer a transportation facility, and reduce fine arts/athletics projects.

title: Amy Coleman Middle School Construction
schools_affected: Amy Coleman Middle School (MS #16, new campus in Fresno area)
description: A 235,325 sq ft, two-story facility with two gymnasiums, two football fields, and four tennis courts. Named after the district's first Black female principal. Bond-funded. Will rebalance enrollment from two existing middle schools.

date: December 2025 (draft plans released); decision expected March 2026
title: Proposed Closure of 7 Elementary Schools + Redistricting
